entry.title: How This Blog Is Built
entry.content:
The whole architecture

src/posts/*.md  --[pandoc]-->  HTML fragment  --[build.mjs + layout]-->  docs/*.html

The entire build dependency is pandoc plus a single Node script that uses nothing but the standard library. There is no node_modules, no bundler, no framework — and the browser receives zero JavaScript.

Repository layout

blog/
├── site.json                 site title, author, base URL
├── build.mjs                 the build script
├── filters/sidenotes.lua     footnote -> margin note
├── templates/layout.html     page skeleton
├── assets/
│   ├── style.css             all styling
│   └── fonts/et-book/        the text typeface
├── src/posts/                your Markdown
└── docs/                     build output (published)

Why Pandoc

After trying the usual static site generators, this came down to three concrete properties:

  1. Math works out of the box. --mathml emits real MathML, which browsers have rendered natively since Chromium 109. No KaTeX, no MathJax, no half-megabyte of runtime.
  2. Highlighting happens at build time. Skylighting tags each token with a class, so colour is entirely a CSS concern — which is what makes light and dark themes a single stylesheet instead of two.
  3. The Markdown dialect is strong enough. GFM plus math extensions covers tables, task lists, footnotes, and definition lists, and matches what GitHub renders for the same file.

How the build works

Each post is compiled twice by Pandoc: once to JSON to read the front matter, once to HTML for the body. Then a handful of post-processing steps run on the output:

// Block math arrives wrapped in a paragraph; unwrap it so it can be
// laid out at the column width rather than inheriting paragraph margins.
html = html.replace(/<p>(<math display="block"[\s\S]*?<\/math>)<\/p>/g, '$1');

// Tables get a scroll container so wide ones don't break the layout on phones.
html = html.replace(/<table(\s|>)/g, '<div class="table-wrapper"><table$1')
           .replace(/<\/table>/g, '</table></div>');

Footnotes are converted to Tufte-style margin notes by a Lua filter, which runs inside Pandoc — so no extra tooling is involved. The filter operates on the AST rather than on rendered HTML, which means the notes end up in the correct position by construction instead of by regex surgery.

The trade-offs

Being honest about what this gives up:

  • No theme ecosystem. Styling is one CSS file you own end to end.
  • No built-in features. Tags, the archive, and the feed are generated by about sixty lines of string concatenation in build.mjs. Easy to change, and yours to maintain.
  • Pandoc's dialect is wider than GFM. Syntax that Pandoc understands but GitHub does not will render on the site and break in the repository view. Worth knowing when a post is meant to be readable in both places.

For a personal blog, that trade buys something worth having: no build cache to clear, no plugin conflicts to debug, no major-version migration to schedule.

Further reading

  • Pandoc manual
  • MathML browser support
  • Skylighting token classes

entry.title: Rendering Mathematics Without JavaScript
entry.content:
The decade of the JavaScript renderer

For most of the web's history, putting a formula on a page meant shipping a renderer. You wrote $E = mc^2$, and some library — MathJax, then KaTeX — scanned the DOM at load time and replaced your plain text with nested <span> elements positioned by hand-tuned CSS.

This worked, and worked well. It is still how most mathematical blogs do it today: I checked a handful of well-known ones and found MathJax 2.7.x on four of them, KaTeX on one.Scott Aaronson's blog loads MathJax 2.7.9 from cdnjs; Math ∩ Programming uses MathJax 3; Math3ma uses 2.7.4; MathOverflow uses 2.7.5. Distill is the KaTeX outlier. Terence Tao's blog takes a different route entirely — WordPress renders each formula to a PNG on the server. But it was always a workaround for a gap in the platform.

The costs are real. MathJax 3 weighs in around half a megabyte and blocks rendering until every expression has been typeset, which is why so many sites show a flash of raw \frac{a}{b} before the page settles. KaTeX is considerably faster and lighter, but covers a smaller slice of LaTeX, and it still requires shipping JavaScript, CSS, and a directory of web fonts.

What changed

MathML — the markup language specifically designed to describe mathematics — has been in browsers for a long time, but Chromium's support was missing for years, which made it useless in practice.

Browser MathML support since
Firefox 4 (2011)
Safari 5.1 (2011)
Chrome 109 (January 2023)
Edge 109 (January 2023)

Once Chromium shipped it, the picture changed quickly. In July 2025 MathML entered Baseline: widely available, which is the standards community's way of saying that every current browser supports it.

That means a formula can now be sent as actual markup:

<math display="inline">
  <semantics>
    <mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow>
    <annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E = mc^2</annotation>
  </semantics>
</math>

The browser renders it natively. No script tag, no font directory, no flash of unstyled TeX.

The trade-off, stated honestly

MathML is not a strict upgrade. Rendering quality still varies between engines, and Chromium's layout is noticeably less polished than KaTeX for anything complicated — matrices, multi-line alignments, nested fractions.

The difference shows up in the sum

(AB)ij=∑k=1naikbkj (AB)_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{ik}\,b_{kj}

only mildly, but a matrix with tall entries is where it becomes visible:

(1x1⋯x1n−11x2⋯x2n−1⋮⋮⋱⋮1xn⋯xnn−1)=∏1≤i<j≤n(xj−xi) \begin{pmatrix} 1 & x_1 & \cdots & x_1^{n-1} \\ 1 & x_2 & \cdots & x_2^{n-1} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 1 & x_n & \cdots & x_n^{n-1} \end{pmatrix} = \prod_{1 \le i < j \le n} (x_j - x_i)

For linear algebra and short derivations, native rendering is entirely serviceable. For a paper full of align environments, it is not yet a substitute.

What you gain is worth listing, because it is not only about bytes:

  • Nothing to execute. The page is HTML and CSS.
  • Text is selectable. A formula is characters, not an image.
  • Screen readers can read it. MathML carries semantic structure that a PNG cannot.
  • It follows your theme. Colour is inherited, so dark mode works without a second render.
  • It degrades gracefully. With CSS disabled you still see meaningful markup.

Adding it to a static site

With Pandoc the whole change is one flag. Write Markdown as usual:

$$
(AB)_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{ik} b_{kj}
$$

and ask for MathML on the way out:

pandoc -f gfm+tex_math_dollars -t html --mathml --wrap=none post.md

The output is what you saw above. Note that gfm already enables tex_math_dollars, so the explicit extension is only there for clarity.

A note on --wrap=none: Pandoc's default line wrapping inserts newlines at 80 columns, and in HTML a newline is whitespace. That matters less than it sounds — Pandoc breaks on spaces, and Chinese text has none, so CJK paragraphs pass through untouched. It is mostly a tidiness flag.

When to reach for a renderer instead

Native MathML is the right default for a personal technical blog. It is the wrong choice in two cases:

  1. You need the full LaTeX surface. Custom macros, \newcommand, AMS environments with numbering, tikz-adjacent packages — KaTeX and MathJax cover far more of it.
  2. You need pixel-identical output across browsers. Native rendering hands layout to the engine, and engines disagree. A client-side renderer produces the same DOM everywhere.

For everyone else — which is most of us writing about algorithms, systems, and the occasional matrix — the trade has finally gone the other way.

entry.title: Math Rendering Reference
entry.content:
Matrices and vectors

A product of two matrices, and a column vector:

A=(1234),v→=(123) A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \vec{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}

Written elementwise:

(AB)ij=∑k=1naikbkj (AB)_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{ik} b_{kj}

Determinants

det⁡A=∣abcd∣=ad−bc \det A = \begin{vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{vmatrix} = ad - bc

The Vandermonde determinant — deliberately wide, to exercise horizontal scrolling on narrow screens:

(1x1⋯x1n−11x2⋯x2n−1⋮⋮⋱⋮1xn⋯xnn−1)=∏1≤i<j≤n(xj−xi) \begin{pmatrix} 1 & x_1 & \cdots & x_1^{n-1} \\ 1 & x_2 & \cdots & x_2^{n-1} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 1 & x_n & \cdots & x_n^{n-1} \end{pmatrix} = \prod_{1 \leq i < j \leq n} (x_j - x_i)

Piecewise definitions and limits

f(x)={x2if x≥0−xotherwise f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 & \text{if } x \geq 0 \\ -x & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} limn→∞(1+1n)n=e \lim_{n \to \infty} \left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)^n = e

Inline math

The complexity 𝒪(nlog⁡n)\mathcal{O}(n \log n) beats 𝒪(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^2). The Euclidean norm of v→\vec{v} is written ∥v→∥2\|\vec{v}\|_2, and the positive reals are ℝ>0\mathbb{R}_{>0}.

Note how inline math sits on the baseline without disturbing the leading of the surrounding paragraph, even when the expression is tall like a+bc+d\frac{a+b}{c+d}.

Code blocks

Plain, unhighlighted:

plain text, no highlighting

C:

#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    char *s = "hello";
    printf("%s\n", s);   // comment
    return 0;
}

Rust:

fn gcd(a: u64, b: u64) -> u64 {
    if b == 0 { a } else { gcd(b, a % b) }
}

Shell:

find . -name '*.md' -exec pandoc -t html {} \;

Python:

from pathlib import Path

posts = sorted(Path("src/posts").glob("*.md"))
for p in posts:
    print(p.stem, p.stat().st_size)

∑\sum summation ∑i=1ni\sum_{i=1}^n i
∏\prod product ∏i=1nxi\prod_{i=1}^n x_i
